title: Resource-oriented REST URLs and CRUD contracts / FastAPI application and path-operation declarations

blocks.text: The path identifies the resource; the method supplies the operation. A collection has no item identifier, while an item path includes one.
GET retrieves, POST performs collection-specific creation processing, PUT replaces the target and DELETE removes it.
A creation contract can pair 201 with a Location identifying the created resource. An absent item can use 404.

edges.label: GET retrieves; PUT replaces; DELETE removes

blocks.alt_text: The collection has no item identifier. The identified item has one; methods supply distinct operations and creation and absence have separate response contracts.

blocks.text: Use /orders for the collection and /orders/{order_id} for an item. GET and PUT address the same item but request retrieval and replacement respectively. POST on the collection can express creation processing; DELETE on the item expresses removal.
For creation, the contract can pair 201 with Location /orders/42; for an absent item, it can use 404. The path alone never completes the operation definition: keep the method alongside it.

blocks.text: Create a FastAPI instance, then use @app.get, @app.post, @app.put or @app.delete with the intended path to register its handler. Method plus path defines the operation, so GET and PUT on one path remain distinct.
Routes are evaluated in declaration order. Put a fixed route before a conflicting parameterized route so the latter does not capture it.

annotations.text: Fixed GET appears before the conflicting parameterized GET.
GET retrieval: same path as PUT, different operation.
PUT replacement and its replace_order handler.
DELETE removal and its remove_order handler.

blocks.text: A request to /orders/current can match /orders/{order_id} if that conflicting declaration comes first. A later fixed declaration does not automatically win. Move the fixed route first.
Separately, GET and PUT on the same item path are different operations. Review method, path and declaration order rather than relying only on how specific the path looks.
Use @app.get for retrieval and @app.put for replacement on the item path. Matching path text does not merge these operations: their methods differ.

For /orders/current and /orders/{order_id}, declaration order matters. Declare the fixed GET first, then the conflicting parameterized GET. Trace the registered method-and-path operation and the first matching route; do not assume a fixed route is always preferred.

segments.label: Create a FastAPI instance and register a GET handler
segments.summary: Import FastAPI and create the application instance with app = FastAPI(). The application object provides decorators for registering handlers. Applying @app.get("/") to a function registers it for GET requests at the root path. The example handler returns a dictionary containing a greeting. A brief editor detour corrects the selected Python interpreter so the import resolves.

blocks.group_title: Create the application and declare a path operation

bridge.before: Watch how the application instance, method decorator, path string and handler fit together. The creator calls this a route; Devspace identifies the method-and-path combination as a path operation.
bridge.after: The clip demonstrates GET registration. The text also covers POST, PUT and DELETE, explains different methods on the same path, and teaches fixed-before-parameterized declaration order, which the clip does not address.

steps.title: Check: FastAPI application and path-operation declarations

public.prompt: GET and PUT are registered on /orders/{order_id}. How many distinct path operations do these declarations represent?

options.text: Two: each method-and-path pair is a distinct operation.
Two, but only the first method declared can serve that path.
One: sharing the path makes the handlers the same operation.

o1.message: A path operation is the combination of an HTTP method and a path; handlers registered for different methods on the same path serve different operations.

o2.message: Different HTTP methods on the same path serve different operations; declaration order does not erase the other method.

o3.message: An operation combines a method and path; sharing a path does not merge methods.

correct.message: A path operation is the combination of an HTTP method and a path; handlers registered for different methods on the same path serve different operations.

incorrect.message: Review the distinction and try again. A path operation is the combination of an HTTP method and a path; handlers registered for different methods on the same path serve different operations.

hints: Identify both parts of a path operation.

steps.title: Check: FastAPI application and path-operation declarations

public.prompt: A GET /orders/{order_id} route is declared before GET /orders/current, with no input conversion restrictions. Which route first captures GET /orders/current?

options.text: The fixed GET route, regardless of declaration order.
The parameterized GET route, because it is evaluated first and matches current.
Neither route: fixed and parameterized routes cannot share a prefix.

o1.message: Routes are evaluated in order; specificity does not override the earlier conflicting match.

o2.message: Routes are evaluated in order, so declare a fixed path before a conflicting parameterized path to prevent the latter from capturing it.

o3.message: A fixed route can coexist with a parameterized one; declare the fixed route first to prevent capture.

correct.message: Routes are evaluated in order, so declare a fixed path before a conflicting parameterized path to prevent the latter from capturing it.
